← Stucco / EIFS repair bid calculator

How much to charge for stucco repair

The number a homeowner wants is a price per square foot, or a published “$12 stucco repair.” That number is not a takeoff. Forty feet of first-story hairline crack on hard-coat, no scaffold, is not the same job as 180 square feet of second-story EIFS torn back to the substrate with new mesh and four window flashings. The wall is still “stucco.” The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the tear-off and the stories, not just the wall area

Siding calculators price a cladding replacement. Exterior-painting calculators price a coating on an intact surface. Foundation-repair calculators price structure. A stucco repair is a finish system: the crack, the hollow, the tear-off, the story, and the flashings. Quoting all of that from a published per-square-foot number is how the first second-story lift eats the field margin.

A job with the same word “stucco” can cost much more

Each second-story elevation is a lift day that never appears on a square-foot sheet. EIFS mesh and lamina are billed as their own hours and their own kit. Window flashing, color match, and a moisture investigation are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 180-square-foot second-story EIFS tear-off with 40 square feet of hollow, four flashings, moisture investigation, and color match prices about $11,941 ($54 per square foot of hollow plus tear-off, 105.1 crew-hours). The same shop’s 40-foot first-story hard-coat crack patch prices about $998 ($25 per crack foot, 7.6 hours, walk-away $718). Matching the brochure job’s per-foot number on the EIFS tear-off is how that job becomes a loss.

A 400-square-foot three-story hard-coat is not automatically the expensive one per foot

A 400-square-foot three-story hard-coat tear-off with gable access is not the EIFS job plus 100%. On the sample rates that elevation prices about $15,829 ($40 per square foot, 147.7 crew-hours) — more money than the EIFS job, but a lower per-foot number, because the mesh, moisture investigation, and four flashings do not live in a published per-square-foot rate. An 80-square-foot first-story one-coat delamination with color match and one flashing prices about $3,050 (25.6 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first lift day.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h plasterer loaded at 32% payroll burden is $50.16. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a stucco specification, a moisture determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. System, substrate, flashing, color match, and whether the wall is holding water are yours to confirm.

Price your stucco repair

Common questions

How much to charge for stucco repair?

Charge from crack linear feet, hollow / delaminated square feet, tear-off to the substrate, stories and scaffolding, window flashing, color match, moisture investigation, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 40-foot first-story hard-coat crack patch at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $998 — about $25 per crack foot.

Why is a per-square-foot stucco quote dangerous?

Homeowners count wall area. Scaffolding, tear-off to the substrate, EIFS mesh, window flashing, color match, and moisture investigation do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper per-square-foot quote written for a brochure crack patch is how a second-story EIFS job becomes a two-day loss.

Does more square footage always cost more to repair?

Not in proportion. On the sample rates a 180-square-foot second-story EIFS tear-off with 40 square feet of hollow, four flashings, moisture investigation, and color match prices around $11,941 ($54 per square foot of hollow plus tear-off), while a 40-foot first-story crack patch prices around $998 ($25 per crack foot).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not construction, engineering, moisture, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Where the hours go

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a stucco specification, or a moisture determination — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why is labor almost three times the material here?

      Because stucco repair is skilled hand work on cheap materials. The default job is $381.22 of labor over 7.6 hours against $143 of material — mostly $44 of mix and $24 of caulk. It is the reverse of most trades on this site, and it means your bid is decided by how accurately you estimated hours, not by what you paid at the supply house. Under-estimating access or cure time hurts here in a way an equipment-heavy job would absorb.

      Why is “price per repair square foot” blank?

      Because the default job is priced by crack length, not area: 40 linear feet of cracking and 20 of caulk, with no delamination or tear-off square footage entered. The per-square-foot figure only appears once you enter repair area. The crack figure it does show, $24.94 per linear foot, is a division of the finished price and falls as the run lengthens — the site time and travel are the same whether you chase 40 feet or 100.

      Why is there a $75 permit on a crack repair?

      Because it is an editable default, not a claim that your job needs one. Cosmetic patching rarely requires a permit; re-lathing a wall or anything touching the weather-resistive barrier often does, and in some jurisdictions any exterior work over a threshold value does. Set it to zero when it does not apply — it is a straight pass-through with no hours attached.

      Should I quote before investigating moisture?

      Usually not, and the option is there for that reason. Cracking and delamination are frequently symptoms of water getting behind the stucco through failed flashing or window details. Patching over that hides the problem for one season and puts your name on it. The moisture-investigation option prices a look first; if you skip it, say in the proposal that the price covers the visible defect only and that concealed damage is a change order.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Stucco Repair Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

“$12 a square foot, done” is not a price for a stucco repair — it is a price for one job's access and tear-off, quietly reused for every wall that gets called in, including the ones with no square footage to multiply at all.

What a flat rate per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote a stucco call over the phone: multiply the repair area by a number and read it back. Homeowners and estimator sheets alike shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of job — usually a ground-level patch on one system, no tear-off, no scaffold, no moisture work — and then reused for every wall afterward, whether or not the next one needs a scaffold lift, a full tear-off to the substrate with new mesh, a moisture investigation, several window flashings, or isn't measured in square feet at all.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter crack linear feet, hollow / delaminated square feet, tear-off square feet, the system (hard-coat, one-coat, or EIFS), the story count, window flashings, color match, and a moisture investigation, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, travel, and target margin. It prices the crack, hollow, and tear-off hours separately, adds scaffold and extra-story hours as their own line rather than a percentage of area, and prices flashing, color match, and moisture work as their own hours and kits, then returns the job price, the walk-away price, and (when there is repair square footage to divide by) the price per square foot — for this wall and this job, not a flat number for every wall.

What a flat rate per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate whether the repair is a hollow cut-out or a full tear-off to the substrate, even though a tear-off needs new mesh over the whole area and more hours per square foot. Prices hollow-repair hours and tear-off hours separately by square footage, and full mesh on the tear-off against patch mesh on the hollow cut-out.
Has no line for whether the wall needs a scaffold or a third-story gable lift — a one-story ladder job and a second-story scaffold job get the same square-foot rate. Prices scaffold and extra-story hours by story count as their own line, since access hours do not scale with wall area.
Has no line for a moisture investigation, window flashings, or color match — a job needing all three gets the same number as one needing none. Prices moisture investigation, each window flashing, and color match as their own hours and kits.
Cannot be applied at all to a crack-only job, since hairline cracking is priced by linear feet, not area. Prices crack feet on their own hours and material line, and reports the price per crack foot instead of a blank square-foot figure.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the price per square foot (or per crack foot), so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two jobs, one flat rate

Using this calculator's own shipped starting examples:

An 80 sq ft first-story one-coat delamination patch, 30 lf of cracks, one window flashing, and a color match, costs $2,195.99 to run, and this calculator prices it at $3,049.99 — $38.12 per square foot.

Take a 220 sq ft second-story EIFS job instead — 40 sq ft hollow plus a 180 sq ft tear-off to the substrate, four window flashings, a moisture investigation, and a color match — and the job costs $8,597.71 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $11,941.26: $54.28 per square foot, about 1.4 times the first job's rate on not quite three times the area. Quoting the EIFS job at the first job's flat $38.12-per-square-foot rate prices it at $8,387.47 — $210.24 below its own break-even cost, before counting the $3,553.79 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 28% target margin. Similar in kind, on paper, and one wall that loses money the moment the scaffold, the tear-off, and the moisture investigation show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot get a stucco repair wrong?

Because the cost driver is the access, the tear-off, and the extras, not the repair area. An 80 sq ft first-story one-coat delamination patch with one window flashing is a short crew visit off a ladder. A 220 sq ft second-story EIFS job -- 40 sq ft hollow plus 180 sq ft torn back to the substrate, four window flashings, a moisture investigation, and a color match -- needs a scaffold lift, new mesh over the whole tear-off, and hours that do not scale with the wall area at all. A flat rate per square foot charges both the same because it was priced on area, not on access, tear-off, or extras.

What does a flat rate per square foot usually leave out entirely?

Whether the story needs a scaffold, whether the repair is a hollow cut-out or a full tear-off to the substrate needing new mesh, and whether there is a moisture investigation, window flashings, or a color match at all. It also has no answer for a crack-only job: forty feet of hairline cracking on hard-coat has no square footage to multiply a rate against, so a per-square-foot number cannot even be applied to a large share of real calls. A flat rate has no line for any of that -- it was set on one job's area and reused for every wall after.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting examples: an 80 sq ft first-story one-coat delamination patch, 30 lf of cracks, one window flashing, and a color match, costs $2,195.99 to run and this calculator prices it at $3,049.99 -- $38.12 per square foot. A 220 sq ft second-story EIFS job -- 40 sq ft hollow plus a 180 sq ft tear-off, four flashings, a moisture investigation, and a color match -- costs $8,597.71 to run and prices at $11,941.26: $54.28 per square foot, about 1.4 times the first job's rate on not quite three times the area. Quoting the EIFS job at the smaller job's flat $38.12-per-square-foot rate prices it at $8,387.47 -- $210.24 below its own break-even cost before a dollar of labor or material is covered, and $3,553.79 short of this calculator's own price at a 28% target margin.

Is a flat rate per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- ground-level, one system, no tear-off, no scaffold, no moisture work -- a flat per-square-foot number can land close, because that is probably the job the rate was set on. The risk is quoting a second-story or tear-off job, a job needing a moisture investigation or several window flashings, or a crack-only job with no square footage at all, the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the access, the tear-off, or the extras until someone is on the wall.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supply house's pricing. It takes the crack feet, hollow area, tear-off, stories, flashings, color match, and moisture investigation, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, travel, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this wall -- the arithmetic a flat rate per square foot skips, not a market survey.

Open the Stucco Repair Bid Calculator to price your own wall, or read how much to charge for stucco repair.

No warranty. This free tool is not construction, engineering, moisture, legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a structural assessment, a specification, or a moisture determination. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, material costs, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked examples.

Free and open source. If it wins you a job, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this stucco or EIFS repair cost, given its cracks, tear-off, stories, and flashing, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes crack linear feet, hollow area, tear-off to the substrate, stories and scaffolding, window flashing, color match, and moisture investigation, plus loaded wage, material rates, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a breakdown of where the hours and cost actually go — including the hours the first second-story lift alone consumes — and a copyable customer-facing bid summary, plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
